images.text:
When Martin Luther King became a leader of the Civil Rights Movement, the laws of segregation had existed since the 1700s.
Since then, the name Martin Luther King has become synonymous with the Civil Rights Movement in America. He inspired and led people in civil rights movements so that they would believe in themselves and it would gain them some momentum.
Martin Luther King was born into an era that demanded great change. When he was ordained a minister at age 17, he had begun the pursuit of making Americans believe that all people were created equal. Later when doing his PhD degree in philosophy, he read the works of Mohandas K. Gandhi and was influenced by the concept of nonviolent protests.

Not long after, King was involved in a peaceful protest in order to oppose segregation and have the laws changed. This was after the Rosa Parks incident on December 1st, 1955. During the protest, his home was bombed and he was arrested.
On August 28, 1963, Martin Luther King went to Washington, DC, so as to lead the "March on Washington". Over 250,000 people from all over the US had joined the historic demonstration when Martin Luther King gave his famous speech, "I Have a Dream." When King won the Nobel Prize the next year, a law ending inequality in hotels and other public places had been passed. Four years later, he organized another big march on Washington – a march for poor people -- so that the government would provide better low-cost housing, jobs, and welfare plans for the poor.

On April 4, 1968,  when he came to Memphis, Tennessee, so that he could gather support for the march, King was shot and killed outside of his hotel. Over 100,000 people attended his funeral in Atlanta. An escaped convict, James Earl Ray, was arrested for the crime and sentenced to 99 years in prison. Martin Luther King was only 39 when he was assassinated, but he will remain an American hero for years to come.

The Past Perfect with When
You can talk about past events that occurred before other events in the past by using the past perfect.
If you want to refer to an earlier action in the past, you can use the past perfect.
<span class="underline">How to form the Past Perfect:
had + past participle
You can also shorten had to 'd.

Example:
I visited Spain with my family in 2003. I went to Spain on my honeymoon in 2007.
I had visited Spain with my family before I went there on my honeymoon.
I'd visited Spain with my family before I went there on my honeymoon.
You can also use the past perfect in sentences with when.
You can use when + simple past + simple past in the main clause as well, but the meaning is different.

When I got home, my mother had made dinner. (My mother made dinner before I got home.)
When I got home, my mother made dinner. (I got home and then my mother made dinner.)
You can also use words like immediately, as soon as and the moment with this structure to show that the action was completed before the other action in the past.

When I had eaten dinner, my mother served dessert. (I finished eating dinner and then my mother served dessert. Dinner was completed.)
As soon as I had eaten dinner, my mother served dessert. (I finished eating dinner and then my mother served dessert. Dinner was completed.)
When I ate dinner, my mother served dessert. (When I started eating, my mother served dessert.)

In the sentences with when + simple past + simple past in the main clause, it is understood which action happens first. Therefore, it is not always necessary to use the past perfect here. We use the past perfect to emphasize the completion of the action before another action.
When Martin Luther King became a leader of the civil rights movement, the laws of segregation had existed since the 1700s.
When he was ordained a minister at age 17, he had begun the pursuit of making Americans believe that all people were created equal.
The Purpose Clause
You can use a purpose clause to talk about why something happens. A purpose is a reason why something is done.
If you want to explain why something happens, you can form a purpose clause with the following structures:

so that + will/would + base form of verb
so that + can/could + base form of verb
Here, can/could = will/ would be able to

• Many people learn a foreign language so that they can improve their chances of finding a job.
  • I lifted my little sister up so that she could reach the top shelf of the cupboard.
  • Laura always makes extra food so that she will have leftovers the next day.
  • I ironed my outfit for work yesterday so that I would be on time this morning.
If the verb is in a present, present perfect or future tense, you need to use can or will. If the verb is in a past tense, then you use could or would.

You can also use the structures:
so that/in order that/that + may/might + base form of verb
so that/in order that/that + shall/should + base form of verb

• My mother always tells us stories about our family so that/in order that/that my siblings and I may remember our family history and pass on the stories.
  • My grandfather renovated his house and added extra rooms so that/in order that/that all his grandchildren might have a place to stay on vacation.

If the verb is in a present, present perfect or future tense, you need to use may or shall. May is more commonly used, however. If the verb is in a past tense, then you use might or should. These make the purpose clause more formal.

You can also use a purpose clause if you want to talk about why something doesn't happen.
For a negative purpose clause you form the negative of the auxiliary verbs (mostly will or would):
so that + will not/won't/wouldn't + base form of verb

• It is a good idea to make a list before you go to the supermarket so that you won't forget to buy anything.
  • I gave Maria an extra blanket so that she wouldn't feel cold during the night.

Another way to make the negative purpose clause would be to change the words in the structure completely.
to prevent + pronoun + gerund
to avoid + gerund

• It is a good idea to make a list before you go to the supermarket to avoid forgetting to buy anything.
  • I gave Maria an extra blanket to prevent her from feeling cold during the night.
These structures are more frequently used and preferred to the negative of the auxiliary verbs as above.
